articles.title: Maresca: “Merecimos algo más, incluso con 3-0 en contra”
articles.standfirst: El técnico italiano habló en TNT tras la derrota ante el PSG
articles.summary: El técnico italiano habló en TNT tras la derrota ante el PSG
articles.body: Enzo Maresca no terminó satisfecho con el resultado ante el PSG. El entrenador del Manchester City considera que su equipo mereció más, especialmente por su rendimiento en la segunda mitad, y lamentó que dos goles en apenas dos minutos complicaran el encuentro. “Empezamos bien, pero encajamos dos goles rápidos y eso generó malas sensaciones. En la segunda parte estuvimos mucho mejor y merecimos algo más”, explicó el técnico citizen tras el partido. El técnico italiano reconoció que el partido se puso cuesta arriba tras los tantos consecutivos del conjunto parisino, pese al buen inicio de los ‘skyblues’. “Hasta el primer gol estábamos jugando bien y dentro del partido. Era muy difícil y, cuando encajas dos goles en dos minutos, todo se vuelve aún peor”, señaló. Maresca también destacó los ajustes realizados al descanso, tanto en la presión como con balón, sin perder el equilibrio del equipo. “Merecimos algo más, incluso con el 3-0 en contra y la cantidad de ocasiones que creamos”, insistió el entrenador, que desveló además las palabras de Luis Enrique al término del encuentro. Según Maresca, el técnico del PSG reconoció que su equipo había tenido fortuna. “Fue sincero al final del partido y dijo que hoy habían tenido bastante suerte".

articles.title: El vestuario se vuelca con Vini: "Sabíamos que no serían dos partidos, es de locos lo que hacen con él"
articles.standfirst: Endrick reflejó tras el encuentro el sentir de los jugadores del Madrid con la sanción del brasileño
articles.summary: Endrick reflejó tras el encuentro el sentir de los jugadores del Madrid con la sanción del brasileño
articles.body: En sus horas más bajas, lejos de su mejor estado de forma y con una sanción de cuatro partidos a cuestas, Vinicius encontró el cariño de sus compañeros. Saben que no lo está pasando bien y todos le arroparon. Endrick, tras el partido ante la Roma, resumía el sentir del vestuario con el castigo impuesto por el Comité de Competición: "Nosotros sabíamos que tenían que ser dos partidos, pero al final de nuestro corazón sabíamos que no iban a ser dos... Porque lo que hacen con Vini es una cosa de locos y esto no va a cambiar, sabíamos que iba a ser así, que iban a buscar a Vini. Es un chico fuerte que siempre lucha contra todo y cuando vuelva va a volver muy bien". Mourinho, antes del partido, no quería valorar el número de encuentros, pero sí cuestionaba el momento. "¿Por qué lo publican dos horas antes de un partido de Champions tan importante?". En el Real Madrid estaban indignados con los cuatro partidos de sanción al brasileño.

articles.title: El gesto de Mourinho tras el 2-1 que sentenció a Vinicius
articles.standfirst: Al técnico luso no le gustó nada el tacón del brasileño que precedió al gol de la Roma
articles.summary: Al técnico luso no le gustó nada el tacón del brasileño que precedió al gol de la Roma
articles.body: El 3-4 del Real Madrid en Roma dejó una imagen llamativa en la banda. Mourinho se mostró visiblemente molesto con Vinicius tras el 2-1 de la Roma, un gol que nació de una pérdida del propio brasileño en el centro del campo y que precipitó su sustitución. La jugada se produjo en el minuto 51. Vinicius recibió un pase de Courtois en la medular e intentó un taconazo hacia atrás que no salió. Un jugador de la Roma robó el balón y lanzó la contra que terminó en el segundo tanto de Donyell Malen, que ponía el 2-1 y encarrilaba, en ese momento, el partido para el conjunto italiano. La reacción de Mourinho desde la banda fue inmediata. El entrenador reprodució hasta dos veces el gesto del taconazo, en señal de reproche por la acción que había originado el gol. Vinicius, que vio la queja de su técnico, miró hacia el banquillo y respondió con un “¿Yo?” justo antes de ser reemplazado. El propio Mourinho apuntó a esa acción en la rueda de prensa posterior, pese a la victoria. “Después encajamos un gol que no podemos hacer. No podemos hacer lo que hemos hecho en el centro del campo”, señaló el portugués, en clara alusión a la pérdida que derivó en el 2-1. El reproche se produjo en una noche en la que Vinicius, titular, estuvo muy lejos de encontrar su mejor versión antes de dejar su sitio en el campo a Endrick. El Madrid, pese a todo, acabó dando la vuelta al marcador en los minutos finales para sellar una remontada de mérito en el Olímpico.

articles.title: Gianni Infantino: The key questions facing FIFA president at crunch council meeting
articles.summary: FIFA president Gianni Infantino set to face questions over his abandoned plan to sell stakes in FIFA tournaments to private investors at Thursday’s FIFA Council meeting; he is under pressure to resign but wants re-election in March 2027
articles.body:
The 10am meeting is the first opportunity for the other 36 Council members to question Infantino directly about his secret plan to sell the World Cup behind their backs.

The key questions for Infantino include:

Why didn't he tell the Council about the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal to sell a 20 per cent stake in all future FIFA tournaments to bankers with ties to US President Donald Trump?

Why was the spin-off company, which was set to be set up, valued at only $20bn when this summer's World Cup alone generated $15bn in revenue?

Why were FIFA's 211 member associations each promised a potential $40m from 2027-30 if they approved the plan, when FIFA already has cash reserves of up to $6bn?

Why is FIFA now proposing to set up a $6.3bn development fund for all associations and is the extra money in the fund connected to Infantino's bid to be re-elected president in March next year?

Why has he plunged football into civil war by refusing to resign, and why won't he resign after losing the support of the presidents of UEFA, CONCACAF, and the Asian Football Confederation?

Why was Folarin Balogun allowed to play for the USA in the World Cup against Belgium when he was suspended? How much pressure was Infantino put under by President Trump in a phone call and how much pressure did Infantino put on the FIFA disciplinary committee to let Balogun play?

What is the FIFA Peace Prize and why was it given to President Trump in Washington in December last year?

Is his plan to reform how he runs FIFA just a ploy to silence his critics and stay in power until 2031? Why does FIFA need governance reform 10 years after he was elected president, promising to reform governance?

Why do US Internal Revenue Service records show he was paid $1.7m in 2024 without FIFA mentioning it in its annual report?

Infantino was at the height of his powers this summer, but he is now facing the most serious crisis of his presidency. Despite the scandals and controversy, though, he will stay in power and win a fourth presidential term if no rival emerges to challenge him before the November 18 deadline.

Infantino had more than 200 letters of support this summer for his re-election bid, including from the English FA, before news broke of his controversial World Cup part-privatisation plan. The plan was quickly abandoned, but many associations, especially in Europe, have withdrawn their letters of support.

The president is elected by FIFA's 211 member associations and Infantino is currently well placed to receive the 106 votes he would need to carry on until 2031. Infantino has not faced any challengers in the two elections since he first became president in 2016.

Arsene Wenger has emerged as a potential candidate to challenge Infantino, but Wenger has been working with Infantino as FIFA's chief of global football development. The former Arsenal manager is a popular and respected figure worldwide, but it remains to be seen whether he can be persuaded to stand.

FIFA has released the meeting agenda and it promises to be a slow burn, with the most contentious items set for discussion at the end of the gathering of what is effectively the FIFA board.

Review of FIFA Forward Enterprise Proposal

Review of FIFA reserves and financing of member associations

Review of FIFA's disciplinary procedures

The FIFA Council has 37 members made up of:

Eight vice presidents including UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin and the presidents of the other five confederations. FA chair Debbie Hewitt is also a vice president

28 other members elected by the FIFA member associations

articles.title: Luis Enrique: “Con un poco de mala suerte, podríamos haber perdido este partido”
articles.standfirst: El entrenador del PSG hace autocrítica a pesar de llevarse los tres puntos del Etihad
articles.summary: El entrenador del PSG hace autocrítica a pesar de llevarse los tres puntos del Etihad
articles.body: Luis Enrique destacó la superioridad de su equipo en la primera mitad, pero reconoció que sufrieron demasiado tras el descanso. “Creo que en la primera mitad demostramos lo que queremos hacer como equipo contra un buen Manchester City. Creo que fuimos muy superiores”, explicó. Pese a la ventaja de 3-0 al descanso, el entrenador español advirtió de los peligros de dar un partido por ganado antes de tiempo. “No me gusta ir ganando 3-0 al descanso porque uno piensa que el partido está ganado, y un partido de este nivel nunca está realmente ganado”, señaló. La reacción del City complicó el encuentro y obligó al PSG a resistir. “Merecieron marcar más goles. Con un poco de mala suerte, podríamos haber perdido este partido”, reconoció. El técnico del PSG también salió en defensa de Ousmane Dembélé ante las críticas recibidas. “¡Ousmane es Ousmane! ¡Son ustedes, los periodistas, quienes hablan mal de Ousmane!”, respondió Luis Enrique. Por último, preguntado por el próximo enfrentamiento contra el Barcelona, el entrenador asturiano evitó señalar quiénes son los dos mejores equipos del momento y puso el foco en el final de temporada. “No es importante ser los mejores equipos ahora mismo, lo importante es ser los mejores equipos al final de la temporada”, concluyó.

articles.title: PSG on 'different level' - are they building greatest European dynasty?
articles.summary: Paris St-Germain are eyeing a third successive Champions League crown after dismantling Manchester City, but where do they rank against Europe's most dominant clubs?
articles.body:
Some find success sweet but fleeting, others spend years building to the pinnacle, and then there are those whose lasting glory evolves into a dynasty.

After tearing Manchester City apart in large spells of their 4-2 Champions League victory on Wednesday, Paris St-Germain look well on track to join the latter bracket.

The back-to-back European champions sliced through City with astonishing ease to take a 3-0 lead into half-time, and were still able to score another despite a spirited second-half fightback from the Premier League leaders.

After obliterating Inter Milan 5-0 in the 2025 final before squeezing past Arsenal on penalties in last season's showpiece game, Luis Enrique's side are aiming to win a third consecutive European crown.

They would be the fifth team to do so going back to 1956, and just the second in the Champions League era.

"This PSG team are on a different level," Chris Sutton told BBC Radio 5 Live at half-time.

"They have just run all over Manchester City, who haven't been able to string passes together. It's been an absolute pummelling for Man City."

To mark PSG's latest display of attacking excellence, we're looking at how the Parisians compare to those clubs who have enjoyed the most dominant eras in European competition.

Some will point out that football existed before the European Champion Clubs' Cup began in 1955 - so apologies to Stan Cullis' 'world-champion' Wolves outfit and the Mitropa Cup's early Vienna heavyweights.

However, this top 10 debate is centred around winning European football's grandest prize.

OK, straight in with the current champions, because this is a dynasty in the making.

Paris St-Germain are hoping to enter that bracket and the 4-2 win against Manchester City on Wednesday reminded the rest of Europe why you shouldn't bet against them becoming continental champions for a third successive season.

PSG had a lacklustre start to the domestic season - they always do, don't they? - but boast an uncanny ability to click into gear when it matters.

In Manchester, Luis Enrique's side were at their unstoppable best. A ruthless blend of silky flicks and slick off-the-ball movement that saw a dazed City caught several frames behind.

"Unbelievable. PSG, what a team," Sutton said.

"PSG's press, I don't think there's another team that press with their intensity and ferocity.

"This [City] is one of the best teams in the Premier League getting an absolutely roasting. This is them [PSG] having a slow start to the season. Heaven help everyone."

The Parisians have been France's most dominant force since the arrival of Qatar Sports Investments 15 years ago, but it took a change of approach for the holy grail of continental success to arrive.

"It's the end of the glitter," professed president Nasser Al-Khelaifi after years of lavish spending, ushering out the "flashy, bling-bling" era.

Instead, Enrique arrived in 2023 intent on building a coherent team. There was still significant investment, but on younger players who could be moulded by his philosophy and discipline while given room to flourish.

The result was two scintillating Champions League triumphs.

Guardiola's return, Man City's defiance - and a game of glorious chaos

Talking of discipline. Helenio Herrera, the Argentine-born defender reared in Casablanca and Paris, had already traversed the dugouts of Atletico Madrid, Malaga, Deportivo and Barcelona before landing in Milan in 1960.

Herrera set about implementing his tactical brand of catenaccio at San Siro - one he insisted is misremembered as being more defensive than it actually was - and developing a ruthless counter-attacking team known as 'Grande Inter'.

Winning the Scudetto in 1962-63, Herrera's outfit became the first to lift the European Cup without losing a game the following season as Sandro Mazzola netted twice against Real Madrid in the final.

The Italians defended their crown the following year, despite losing their semi-final first leg at Anfield, edging Benfica in the final. It was the Portuguese giants' second final defeat in three seasons. Some may say they were cursed...

The story goes that Bela Guttmann, fresh from winning the title with Porto, rocked up at Benfica, sacked all the senior players and promoted a talented bunch of youth team players instead.

Those promising youngsters won the title and then went all the way in the European Cup, beating Barcelona in the 1961 final.

That summer, a teenage Eusebio also joined Guttmann's squad and steered them to European glory once more, seeing off Tottenham Hotspur in the semi-final before beating the great Real Madrid in the competition's showpiece.

The legendary Ferenc Puskas scored a first-half hat-trick for the Spaniards, but Eusebio netted twice after the interval to seal Benfica a second successive crown.

Guttmann, buoyed by his remarkable success, left the club after not being offered the pay rise he felt he deserved and the curse the Hungarian boss supposedly put on the club - that they would not win another European trophy for 100 years - has become fable.

Whether the often-disputed story is true or not, the Lisbon giants have not landed another since - losing eight European finals, including three in the 1960s.

This was Bayern's coming of age. Emerging from what was a fiercely competitive West German football scene, the Bavarians - promoted to the Bundesliga less than a decade earlier - were able to establish themselves as heavyweights in Europe.

With a backbone of goalkeeper Sepp Maier, marauding sweeper Franz Beckenbauer and the prolific Gerd Muller, and fresh off West Germany winning the 1974 World Cup, Bayern clinched three on the bounce, despite their domestic form dipping.

In fact, Beckenbauer said Bayern were past their peak after the first European Cup win over Atletico Madrid, but experience carried them through big games.

They beat Leeds in a controversial final in Paris, and then saw off Saint-Etienne the following year.

The teams above make the list for their trophy-winning spells. Pep Guardiola's Barcelona were European champions twice in three years - losing to Jose Mourinho's treble-winning Inter in between - but their dynasty was built on more than silverware.

Guardiola only spent four seasons at Barcelona, but it was an era-defining tenure, the Catalan giants pioneering a brand of football that would be celebrated and copied the world over.

Perhaps the real success of a team is in its legacy. Guardiola's tiki-taka Barcelona built around La Masia graduates Xavi, Andres Iniesta, Sergio Busquets and, of course, Lionel Messi still resonates more than a decade since he left.

Where does this particular Milan dynasty start and end? It was fuelled, of course, by Silvio Berlusconi, who saved the club from bankruptcy in 1986 and appointed the up-and-coming Arrigo Sacchi as boss.

You could argue it continued until a Champions League final defeat by a young Ajax side in 1995. In between, the Rossoneri won back-to-back European Cups in 1989 and '90, then thrashed Cruyff's Barcelona 'Dream Team' in 1994 after defeat in the final the previous season.

In fact, the only campaigns in which Milan did not reach the final were after their quarter-final second leg was abandoned because of floodlight failure while trailing Marseille in 1991. The Serie A giants' refusal to re-enter the pitch for the final minutes of that one also led to them being banned the following year.

From Sacchi to Fabio Capello, through the brilliant Dutch trio of Ruud Gullit, Marco van Basten and Frank Rijkaard to homegrown stars Franco Baresi, Paolo Maldini and Alessandro Costacurta - the Italian core remaining from that 1989 triumph to the defeat by Ajax six years later - Milan were a phenomenal force.

In an era of English dominance on the continent, winning seven of eight European Cups between 1977 and 1984, Liverpool's 'Boot Room' boys led the way.

The Reds won four of those, Nottingham Forest - who could argue they also deserve a spot on the list - went back-to-back and Aston Villa completed the haul.

Liverpool's European pedigree really began when Bill Shankly's side won the Uefa Cup in 1973, the Reds doing it again three years later under Shankly's former assistant Bob Paisley.

Paisley was able to deliver the biggest prize of all the following season in Rome and, after Kenny Dalglish was brought in to replace Hamburg-bound Kevin Keegan, retained the European Cup at Wembley against Club Brugge in 1978 - the Scottish forward netting the winner.

Three years later, after Brian Clough took Forest to the top, Liverpool were European champions again when Alan Kennedy's goal downed Real Madrid in Paris.

Perhaps most impressive is how the Anfield outfit were able to maintain that success through a series of managers. The line of succession from Shankly to Paisley then landed on Joe Fagan, who was in charge when they beat Roma - in Rome - in '84. That was before the Heysel disaste r, and defeat by Juventus, the following year.

Atletico fans look away now. Two finals in three years and twice Diego Simeone's side ran into their Madrid rivals, losing in agonising fashion in both 2014 and 2016.

The second of those also sparked a three-year winning run for the most successful club in European Cup history.

Real Madrid's formula was seemingly simple: construct a team of the world's best players - spearheaded by Cristiano Ronaldo - and stick a legendary former star in charge.

Zinedine Zidane's new-era galacticos just felt inevitable - they always found a way to win, becoming the first club in the Champions League era not only to retain the trophy but to lift three in a row.

After downing Atletico in the first of the three-peat, they beat Juventus and then Liverpool - the latter remembered for Gareth Bale's cameo, Loris Karius' blunders and Sergio Ramos leaving his mark on Mo Salah.

Similar to Guardiola's Barcelona, the influence of this Ajax side was seen far beyond the trophy cabinet. The lineage of their philosophy - via Johan Cruyff - survives through several of the clubs on this list, from Catalonia to Paris.

Rinus Michels was the pioneer, taking Ajax from the threat of relegation to the most dominant side in Europe, losing the 1969 final to AC Milan but returning to win it for the first time two years later with their swaggering brand of Total Football.

Michels left for Barcelona on the back of that success, though Stefan Kovacs was able to retain the trophy the following year and then add a third successive European crown to Ajax's pile with an impressive run that included knocking out Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and then Juventus in the final.

Cruyff, about to win the second of his three Ballon d'Ors, followed Michels to Barcelona and Ajax's dynasty began to fall apart. The legacy, however, remains.

When it comes to dominance, no one compares to the Real Madrid side who stormed to five successive European Cup triumphs after the competition began in 1955.

With the tournament in its infancy, it was perhaps not considered as imperative by certain nations compared to how Champions League participation dominates clubs' thoughts today, but Real Madrid's style and success helped to alter perceptions.

Alfredo Di Stefano, already a world star by the time Real beat Reims in the inaugural final, was an integral part of the Spanish giants' success, the legendary Paco Gento likewise a stalwart (he also won a sixth European Cup in 1966).

Then, in 1958, Madrid added Hungarian genius Ferenc Puskas following his two-year ban for refusing to return to Budapest after the revolution in 1956.

Puskas was 31 when he joined, but scored 35 goals in 39 European Cup games for Real Madrid, including four in the 7-3 win over Frankfurt at Hampden in the 1960 final. Di Stefano grabbed the other three as Madrid made it five on the spin.

articles.title: Vinicius rompe su silencio: una sanción en "mal momento", los pitos, su enfado y una promesa
articles.standfirst: El brasileño habló tras el Roma - Real Madrid
articles.summary: El brasileño habló tras el Roma - Real Madrid
articles.body: Vinicius Junior rompió su silencio y habló tras conocer los cuatro partidos de sanción que le ha impuesto el Comité de Competición. "Creo que la sanción ha salido en un mal momento. Han tenido todo el día para sacar la sanción y me he enterado al llegar al estadio. La norma es nueva y siempre vienen los de LaLiga a explicarnos las cosas nuevas, pero justamente esto no nos lo han explicado. Nunca he tenido una acción de violencia contra otro jugador. A mí me pegan bastante y la tarjeta siempre es bastante para mí". Una vez analizada su sanción, el brasileño habló de su estado de forma e hizo autocrítica. Fue sincero Vini respecto a su rendimiento: "Normal, me he enfadado después del cambio porque siempre quiero estar bien y ayudar al equipo. Los cambios han cambiado al equipo. Endrick ha cambiado la dinámica y ha sido el mejor. Y Carlos entra pocos minutos pero marca. "Estoy enfadado conmigo mismo por no estar en mi mejor versión. Al final, Vini siempre vuelve y no tengo dudas de que voy a volver". También habló de los pitos del Bernabéu y los asume sin problemas. No le gustan, pero mostró respeto a la afición. "Seguramente los pitos no me ayudan, pero la gente paga sus entradas. Jugamos mejor si tenemos a los aficionados con nosotros. Jude juega mejor, Mbappé juega mejor, yo juego mejor... Creo que es más fácil pitarme a mí porque llevo más tiempo y soy uno de los capitanes". Y por último, lanzó un mensaje: "Voy a volver, cuando llegué joven muchos se rieron de mí y al final llevo más de 100 goles con el Real Madrid". Sobre una supuesta persecución de las aficiones rivales y los árbitros, dijo: "La afición me tiene que pitar porque estoy para meter goles a sus equipos pero los árbitros no lo entiendo, porque he visto un dato que dice que me hacen 500 faltas para cinco tarjetas rojas y no se cuántas amarillas y las amarillas siempre son para Vini, no entiendo, tenemos que defender a los jugadores que lo hacen diferente, como Lamine en el Barcelona o Julián en el Atlético".

articles.title: Aston Villa: Champions League rout proves Villa are finding momentum
articles.summary: Nicolas Jackson continues his fine goalscoring form as Aston Villa record an impressive Champions League win.
articles.body:
Nicolas Jackson celebrated his first-half double by making a cutting motion which proved fitting on a night Aston Villa found their clinical edge.

A first win at Villa Park this season, three first-half goals with six in total and a commanding Champions League victory - all in the biggest European win in their history.

Unai Emery said his side had been impacted by the rebuild of the North Stand after three winless games at home this season but they showed no signs of struggle against Fenerbahce.

A dominant victory against the Turkish visitors leaves Villa already well placed to reach the Champions League knockout phase and will add to their slowly growing momentum.

Questions had been building as Villa picked up just one point from their opening three Premier League home games this season even if Saturday's 2-2 draw with Brentford ensured they avoided a third-straight home league defeat under Emery for the first time since February 2024.

Against Fenerbahce, they found a willing opponent. Scattered with former Premier League players, including Ederson, Nathan Ake, Romelu Lukaku and Nelson Semedo, the visitors would have been a formidable foe five years ago.

Instead, they folded quickly in the first half - despite Zion Suzuki's two important saves - as Johan Manzambi and Jackson's double put Villa in complete control.

The goals came in front of the skeleton of the North Stand, which will not have gone unnoticed as they had previously scored only once when attacking that end this season.

Ross Barkley's double and Tammy Abraham's late tap in added to the visitors' woes and underlined Villa's dominance.

They last scored so many in a 6-1 win over Brighton three years ago and had previously put five past Hibernian in the Europa Conference League in 2023.

The result provides another springboard and extends Villa's recent form to just one defeat in their last seven games.

However, Emery's rebuild will still take time. Before the international break, he described the opening five weeks of the campaign as similar to still being in pre-season with 10 new players to adapt following a chaotic summer of change.

Reflecting post match on how things are now progressing, he said: "They (Fenerbahce) didn't deserve 6-0 but for us it was very important how we achieved the first win at home and how we managed with different players, our progression and step forward.

"There is still a lot of work to do and we need time, we are progressively getting better and it was a good step forward. In the Champions League the three points are important. We want to be a protagonist in the Champions League.

"Now the clear objective is against Newcastle because of the lack of points in the Premier League."

The shoots of progress are already evident.

Manzambi glided past powerless Fenerbahce tackles, Ibraham Mbaye found space to exploit - even if he needs to improve - and Jackson was clinical.

Leon Goretzka made his debut as a late substitute and Suzuki remained commanding, continuing to slip into his role with ease.

"I think that's what Emery has been talking about with the potential of this team and what they can do," former Villa captain Stiliyan Petrov told TNT.

"There's been a lot of questions from the start of the season, even for this game as well. People asking how far they can go in this competition but it seems as though they're clicking together and there's a flow to their game.

"The players that Emery has brought in are starting to perform really well and it's a well-deserved win."

'Jackson is doing a fantastic job, fantastic task'

Record £65m signing Jackson came to replace the departing Ollie Watkins after his £50m switch to Al-Hilal.

He joined having helped Bayern Munich win the Bundesliga last season on loan from Chelsea, and on moving to Villa Park was reunited with Emery.

The pair worked together at Villarreal, with Emery giving him his debut with the Yellow Submarine.

The 25-year-old scored the final goal for Emery at Villarreal before the manager left for Villa in October 2022, a last-minute winner against Almeria, and has repaid the faith quickly on their reunion.

The only thing missing for Jackson was a potential hat-trick, with Barkley - the pre-arranged penalty taker - scoring from the spot.

"I wanted to take it but the most important thing is we win. Hopefully next time I'll get the hat-trick," Jackson told TNT Sports.

"It's very important. We haven't won at home. Our keeper is amazing."

Jackson's four goals in three games and five for the season in total allow Villa and their fans to move on quickly from Watkins, their record Premier League scorer, following a summer exit that threatened to turn acrimonious .

Emery added: "Jackson is doing a fantastic job.

"He's scoring, he's working defensively [and] helping the team. This is very important and maybe in the future he can shoot (from the spot) as well."

Villa, and their new-look forward line, will now be eager for Saturday's trip to Newcastle, especially as Matthias Jaissle's side shipped four against Coventry on Monday to leave them with the joint-worst defensive record in the Premier League.

And Jackson hopes he can prosper alongside his attacking colleagues.

"He [Johan Manzambi] is a top player. I'm really happy we're playing together. I hope we score many more goals together," Jackson said. "[Ibrahim Mbaye] is [also] an amazing player. We're in the [Senegal] national team together and hopefully he'll get more time to play [for Villa]. He's very fast and it's good to have him."

articles.title: Who leads the FBS in receiving yards and touchdowns? Hint: It's not Jeremiah Smith
articles.summary: Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith has gotten much of the hype at the receiver position this season, but the FBS leader in receiving yards and touchdowns plays for...
articles.body:
With all the hype around Jeremiah Smith, one might think the insanely gifted Ohio State wideout would far and away be the nation's leader in receiving yards and touchdown catches.

Meet Oregon State freshman Jesse Legree, who tops the FBS in both categories. He has 932 receiving yards to Smith's 916 and has 12 touchdown receptions to Smith's 11. And he's done it with 10 fewer catches than Smith, boasting an average of 24.5 yards per catch that ranks third nationally.

While Smith is physically imposing at 6-foot-4 and 222 pounds, Legree is doing all this as a freshman who stands only 5-10 and weighs barely 170 pounds.

Legree punches above his weight, so to speak. He has at least 100 yards receiving in every game this season and has helped the Beavers take the national lead in yards passing per game. Behind its explosive offense, Oregon State has compiled a 4-2 record, including four straight wins.

Legree speedster opened the season with five catches for 136 yards and a touchdown against Big 12 contender Houston. The speedster showed that was no fluke with eight catches for 240 yards and two scores against Texas Tech -- a program that reached the College Football Playoff last season.

He followed those eye-opening performances with four catches for 100 yards and a touchdown against Montana and six catches for 109 yards and two scores against UTEP.

He was just getting warmed up. He caught five passes for 156 yards and three scores in a 56-26 win over Colorado State. He then had 10 catches for 191 yards and three more scores in a 66-14 victory over San Diego State. He even hit the Heisman pose after one of his scores against the Aztecs.

Legree benefits from having quarterback Braden Atkinson feed him the ball. Atkinson is a 6-1 sophomore who transferred from Mercer after winning the Jerry Rice Award for the top freshman in the FCS. Atkinson now leads FBS with 2.257 yards passing through six games.

Oregon State's next game is Saturday against Washington State. Legree's best remaining chance to draw national attention will be Nov. 14 at Boise State. If he keeps up his current pace up, he might find himself in New York in December.

articles.title: Man City dismantled by Paris St-Germain in breathless Champions League battle
articles.summary: When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned late...
articles.body:
When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League's independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City's expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG's was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero's club record.

It could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain's armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

"Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis (Enrique, PSG's coach) said at the end of the game that they were quite lucky," Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. "My feeling is we are there. We are close," he added.

Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of "sham" contracts to inflate income this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

There is a certain irony that it was PSG who inflicted this defeat, ending City's run of eight wins from eight in all competitions under Maresca.

It was a meeting of two clubs empowered more than any other by the riches of Gulf states: Abu Dhabi versus Qatar. Both have also had their run-ins over money. Both were sanctioned but escaped full bans by Uefa for breaching Financial Fair Play rules.

The question, also, was: would the eighth meeting of these clubs in the Champions League in the last 11 seasons be the last for some time?

So we should savour it and we did. That included Pep Guardiola on his first return to the Etihad – in a sign of solidarity – after quitting at the end of last season. Not that he savoured much of what he saw as PSG dominated City to such an extent that their fans adopted the "Poznan" celebration and the home supporters were silenced.

City could have gone in front before they conceded with the erratic Safonov – who was Gianluigi Donnarumma's understudy and has become his unlikely replacement – punching a corner against his own crossbar before Antoine Semenyo shot the rebound over.

Then PSG ran all over City. They were never going to come here and not try to win. They broke far too easily and scored far too easily. Not once but twice to go 2-0 up.

For the first, PSG countered, with City struggling to cover, and Doué caught out Donnarumma with a low shot back inside his right-hand post from 22 yards.

Then PSG sliced through City's defence with Ousmane Dembélé scooping the ball across the area to Doué who returned it back. Dembélé stooped to head home.

After Achraf Hakimi headed against the inside of the post, City could not clear, the ball came back with Warren Zaïre-Emery flicking on Maghnes Akliouche's cut-back. It ran to Vitinha who slammed in a first-time shot. It was the first time City had ever conceded three goals at home in the first half of this competition.

Maybe it was too easy. Maybe City could not continue to be so dominated but it was as if a switch was flicked when the teams returned. The chances came for City. Enzo Fernández should have scored from a close-range header and Haaland did, glancing in an inswinging Ndiaye cross.

Finally the City fans found their voices but then they were silenced. What a calamity for Donnarumma as he got a hand to Akliouche's shot on the turn but only palmed the ball up in the air with it bouncing into net.

But City did not stop. Nuno Mendes headed Josko Gvardiol's flick off the line, Fernández hit the post before Bouaddi set up Haaland and he swept the ball past Safonov.

There was time for PSG to miss a penalty, with Donnarumma comfortably saving Ferran Torres's weak effort as City bravely continued to push. They lost but it did not quite feel like that.

I think our start was quite good until the first goal. Then we conceded the second after one [more] minute and that created bad feelings so we struggled.

Second half we were much, much, much better and we probably deserved even something more.

It was strange to be honest because until the first goal we were in the game. We created things, didn't concede and then the first goal led to the second one. When you concede two goals in two minutes it could [get] even worse.

At half-time we adjust something, didn't lose our balance and in the second half we created enough to deserve something more. We adjusted the way we were pressing, something on the ball [too].

We lost the balance [by conceding the second goal]. Even at zero-three we created enough in the second half and Luis said afterwards that they had been quite lucky.

[A message for the fans?] We feel sorry for the first half but I think we're quite happy now. Big game on Saturday [Ipswich at home at 3pm].

Both Arsenal and Barcelona had shorter prices than PSG to win the Champions League. Now it's only Barcelona but I would say even they are not as good as PSG.

I doubt Guardiola will speak publicly but let's wait and see.

Matheus Nunes, Bouaddi and Ndiaye were terrific. Small wonder that Luis Enrique and Maresca were exhaling hard as they embraced at the final whistle.

After a PSG performance in the first half that was as good as any I've seen in the past 10 years, Manchester City stiffened midfield in the second and went toe-to-toe to play their part in a basketball game with crosses and shots raining down on the PSG goal.

PSG have managed this last few minutes well, making important tackles and interceptions.

Pacho cuts out a pass to stop Semenyo pouncing.

City have had 27 attempts on goal, PSG 14.

PSG have dropped back in numbers and City are probing away.

Four minutes to come. O'Reilly replaces Enzo Fernandez.

Ferran Torres hit it low and not even halfway towards the right post. Terrible penalty, straightforward save.

His hand touched the sole of his boot as he slid in. Very soft.

Didn't seen that Matheus Nunes touched Nuno Mendes from the replay.

Semenyo takes Haaland's pass and his iffy control by the right of the penalty spot knocks it up. He does well to manipulate the defender out of the way but the ball won't come down quick enough and he ends up stretching for it and lashes it over the bar.

Anderson, looking for Haaland from the left with a right-foot inswinger, overcooks it and Safonov comes off his line to catch.

Haaland meets Nunes daisycutter of a cross having been sent to the byline with his outstretched left leg as he slides in at the back post and Safonov sprawls to save on the goalline again. Should have scored but then again he was right at the extent of his reach when he made the connection.

Attempts on goal now number 36 after Kvaratskhelia's tepid effort is saved by Donnarumma then Khusanov makes a last gasp tackle to stop Ferran Torres converting Joao Neves's sensational pass.

This is a game for the ages. Too much action to chronicle fairly.

Ferran Torres → Dembele Joao Neves → Akliouche

Man City 2 PSG 4 (Haaland) Having just stuck an effort on to the top of the crossbar, Haaland sweeps a right-foot shot into the bottom left corner after terrific work from Bouaddi to win the ball, play a one-two with Fernandes and tee up the hit man.

Now Anderson floods into space 20 yards out and runs on to a pass to shoot and Pacho again makes the block.

Ndiaye, who has been magic, fizzes a pass into Fernandez's feet and the Argentina midfielder absolutely lashes a right foot shot into the angle of post and bar.

Mendes heads Gvardiol's near-post flick from the free-kick off the line with Safonov stranded.

Ndiaye and Anderson combine and the latter's tenacity is rearded with a free-kick out by the left corner flag when Zaire-Emery boots him.

Haaland blazes over with his left when put through down the inside-left channel by Fernandez's fine pass. Maresca hops in frustration.

Semenyo does well to twist Pacho and Ruix but shoots into the side-netting.

Man City 1 PSG 4 (Akliouche) The winger receives the pass in the D facing the right touchline, spins and puts his laces through a left-foot piledriver. Donnarumma soars to his right, sticks up his top hand and tips it upwards but without enough power to push it over or wide and it drops behind the keeper and spins past the scrambling keeper.

No doubt that PSG have been rattled by City's ferocity in this half so far and have not been able to stop Bouaddi pulling the strings.

Bouaddi to Semenyo who sends Nunes on the underlap to the byline. The right-back fizzes over a cross and Ndiaye sticks out his right leg and just gets his toe to it but cannot hook it on target.

Fernandez drills a lofted pass from the right out to Ndiaye who burns past Hakimi down the outside and tries to but it back to Haaland but Marquinhos telescopes out a leg to knock it away. The crowd is now just electric having flat-lined in the first half.

City have turned the momentum around as they fly forward and create chances for Semenyo and then Haaland and Semenyo, the last two when the flag was poised to go up. Ndiaye is giving Hakimi a roasting.

Man City 1 PSG 3 (Haaland) Header from 12 yards, unstoppable, set up by Ndiaye with a superb cross moments after the substitute had drilled a shot straight at Safonov.

Enzo Fernandez should score with a header at the back post when he meets a cross from the right. He had run off Hakimi and was completely free but diverted it wide, helping it on its way, rather than going back across Safonov.

Semenyo runs on to Haaland's square pass and shoots with his left on the right of the box from 16 yards into a defender. Should have done better. City corner and Gvardiol, who had got away from his marker, pumps his header straight at Safonov.

Bouaddi immediately finds Ndiaye with a crossfield pass to the left and the winger drives towards the box but thrashes his rising shot over the bar.

Nunes → Dias Ndiaye → Doku Bouaddi → Cherki.

It would make sense to stiffen midfield by introducing Bouaddi and trying a different right-back though neither Rico Lewis or Matheus Nunes are defensively sound. Perhaps they should have done that at 2-0. Having said that, City have made four or five half-chances and, although they have been overwhelmed at times, the scoreline could be closer.

Anderson pings a pass out to Doku who dribbles in from the left, burns past Hakimi and then shoots low to Safonov's left.

Marquinhos blocks Semenyo's shot and then Fernandez is tackled as he tries to drive into the box.

Two minutes of stoppage time are signalled as Doku gives the ball away.

PSG corner as their fans sing their favourite Bonnie Tyler song. The ball rolled down Dias's arm but he protests weirdly that it should be a goalkick. From the corner a deflection off Guehi forces Donnarumma into a save.

Chance for City with Gvardiol by the left post but he snatches at it.

City corner after Semenyo's good run. PSG turn it behind at the near post and the second attempt, taken short, is worked to Haaland in the box but he makes a mess of his connection. Just before Hakimi, in acres hectares of free space has a dig and fires his shot straight at Donnarumma.

In the words of Barry Davies. Poor old Man City just don't know what day it is. Hakimi whacks a right-foot shot inches past the left post.

City held a lengthy post-mortem after they conceded a third goal in the first half of a European match for the first time. They can't cope with PSG's three midfielders. Cherki is not built for this.

Man City 0 PSG 3 (Vitinha) A few seconds earlier Hakimi, evading his marker, hit the post with his header after Doué and Vitinha, one outside, inside, had Khusanov chasing shadows. Then PSG win the ball back and work it into the box from the right. Zaire-Emery's backheel puts it perfectly in Vitinha's path and he rockets a shot past Donnarumma and into the backboards behind the goal with a thud.

Donnarumma dives to his right to save Vitinha's shot but can only parry it and back come PSG with such slick passing they manipulate space for their runners to glide into. It's Zaire-Emery's turn to have a shot and Guehi wears it flush in the face.

From the corner Doku has the vision to spot a gap for Anderson to burst into the box but Anderson isn't on the same wavelength and is out of the blocks too late.

Doku, who is playing well, diddles Hakimi with an explosive start from a standstill to drive past him and ping a cross to the back post. Haaland, behind Pacho, can't track the flight properly with the defender blocking his view. In the end he has a free header but saw it so late he can only head it back across goal. Safety firts from PSG who put it behind for a corner.

Haaland tries to force a shot past Pacho who is too close and makes a solid block. Moments later Semenyo, looking for Haaland at the back post, bends a left-foot cross from the right over his head and out for a goal-kick. Haaland shoots him an old-fashioned look.

The freedom Hakimi has to drive into the forward line and stay there is causing Gvardiol all kinds of problems. Out come the raucous away fans' olés.

And just like that… PSG go Bang! Bang! and the crowd falls quiet.

Man City 0 PSG 2 (Dembele) Made by more Doué brilliance. Khusanov can't handle the ghostly movement of Doué who then stands up a terrific cross to the back post and Dembele, running off Gvardiol and Guéhi, buries a header from a couple of yards. Donnarumma had no chance. Ninety-nine seconds between goals.

Man City 0 PSG 1 (Doué) The slickest of moves from their own byline on the right, Hakimi bringing it forward as Gavrdiol jumps into the press too high and cannot get close. PSG work it inside to Akliouche who passes to Ruiz. The Spain midfielder bends a pass with the outside of his left to switch it out to Doué who feigns to whip it into the top right, cocks his ankle and flays it in at the near post.

City whip the free-kick to the near post to Dias and Safonov pulls off the save after a glancing touch from the City captain.

Safonov flaps and the corner whipped under his crossbar and the ball slides off his attempted punch the wrong way and into the bar. It rebounds and drops to Semenyo who blazes over from six yards. But the ref blows his whistle for a foul on the keeper.

Cherki goes over in the PSG box when Marquinhos sticks out his leg and Cherki tumbles over the hurdle. The ref waves play on but VAR has a look and sees that Marquinhos brushed the ball with his studs. City have a free-kick for a foul on Gvardiol.

Loose pass by Semenyo goes straight to Fabian Ruiz who tries to slip Doué in down the left but Dias slides over to intercept. Zaire-Emery feeds on the scraps and shoots straight down Donnarumma's throat.

Vitinha surprises Fernández by feinting to cut inside then knocking it on the outside to Doué down the left but Khusanove forces him to turn tail.

There are a few inflatable bananas being waved around and a cry of "Guardiola" but, in truth, the noise is really coming from the PSG fans in one corner of the stadium. There is certainly no air of defiance or protest aimed at the Premier League – expect for another chant aimed at Sky Sports pundit Gary Neville.

Gvardiol and Khusanov are both pushing into midfield while Fernandez and Anderson drop back to fill in.

Donnarumma leaves a pass to Guehi short but Akliouche kicks him as he tries to recover and City have a free-kick that Donnarumma launches up the left. Hakimi heads it infield and Doku earns a throw-in with a challenge on Fabian Ruiz.

PSG with their usual kick-off, booting it 40 yards up one wing, this time the left and Gvardiol heads it away as the smoke begins to clear.

The pitch at the Etihad Stadium is shrouded in smoke from a firework display just before kick-off. It seems to sum up the lack of clarity around the club at present.

PSG were ready for a good couple of minutes before City turned up.

Die Meister Die Besten Les grandes équipes The champions!

A firework and light show illuminate the stadium

It must be said there are an extremely low number of inflatable bananas on show.

Former manager joins chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano in the directors' box.

Pep Guardiola, wearing a flat cap, has taken his seat in the Manchester City directors' box, directly behind chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana. It is of course his first game back at the club after quitting as manager in the summer. It is also a declared show of solidarity after the guilty verdict.

It's a special night against the best team in Europe, I hope it's a special game. Pep is here but was not at the training ground. I have not spoken with him.

It's a special moment for him also, he is back in his home and the fans will be happy that he is here tonight.

Quite easy decision to bring Jérémy in. The most important think for him is to stay fit that's why he are having to manage his minutes.

I said yesterday you need a complete performance, top on and off the ball to beat them. We will create some chances and concede some chances but you have to find the complete balance.

Under normal circumstances there would be a high level of anticipation around this game, even though it is the eighth time in 11 seasons that City and PSG have faced each other in the Champions League. But given the backdrop of City guilty verdict and it being the first home fixture since that announcement it is even more fascinating. There will also be, of course, Pep Guardiola back "in his house", as his successor, Enzo Maresca. put it. The atmosphere will be interesting.

If the verdicts are upheld, of course, it wasn't their penthouse and it wasn't their caviar.

A City fan on whether City's trophies have asterisks against them

We got to live in a penthouse and eat caviar for 15 years and if we have to go back to a semi in the suburbs, well, fine.

Qatar showed Man City how to build a football superpower

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside .

Joleon Lescott on his reaction to the verdicts

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won't forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Manchester City Donnarumma; Khusanov, Dias, Guéhi, Gvardiol; Anderson, Fernández; Semenyo, Cherki, Doku; Haaland. Substitutes Bettinelli, Rulli, Ndiaye, Kovacic, Aït-Nouri, Reis, Nunes, Bouaddi, O'Reilly, Allan, Foden, Lewis.

Paris Saint-Germain: Safonov; Hakimi, Marquinhos, Pacho, Nuno Mendes; Ruiz, Vitinha, Zaïre-Emery; Doué, Dembélé, Akliouche. Substitutes Chevalier, Mouak, Beraldo, Zabarnyi, Kvaratskhelia, Ferran Torres, Digne, L. Hernández, Godts, Dro Fernández, Ndjantou, João Neves.

Safonov; Hakimi, Marquinhos, Pacho, Nuno Mendes; Zaïre-Emery, Vitinha, Fabián Ruiz; Akliouche, Dembélé, Doué.

That means Luis Enrique, who has the luxury in Ligue 1 to rest many players, makes eight changes from the XI for Saturday's home victory over Le Mans.

Kvaratskhelia is only on the bench, as is the wonderful Joao Neves. That's what you call an embarrassment of riches.

Matheus Nunes and Nico O'Reilly are out at full-back, replaced by Abdukodir Khusanov and Josko Gvardiol, while Jérémy Doku, who came off the bench on Sunday and scored, replaces Iliman Ndiaye:

TNT Sports had a first go at addressing the Manchester City verdicts on Saturday

And it didn't go very well. Joe Cole was remarkably incoherent even for a football pundit talking about more important issues. And words you never thought you would type: Martin Keown the voice of sense:

Luis Enrique on the independent commission's verdict

I hope everything works out well for Man City because I think what they have done on the pitch has been incredible over the last few years and they certainly deserved to win all the trophies they have won.

The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch. They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction.

But now we have to wait to see what the authorities decide or the judge is going to say.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City's conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City's games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don't think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let's get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

PSG have made a slow start to their Ligue 1 campaign, their worst since Luis Enrique's first season in charge. Starting with two draws and a defeat, they have rallied with three successive victories to climb up to sixth as the head coach, as he tends to do in the league, rotates his midfielders and forwards like crazy, to whose ranks he has added the World Cup-winner Ferran Torres. The summer signing scored a hat-trick in his Champions League debut for the club, a 6-1 mauling of Slovan Bratislava.

City, too, started their European campaign with a win, Erling Haaland scoring both goals in the 2-0 victory over Porto at the Dragao and you won't need me to remind you that they have won all six of their Premier League games to lead Arsenal by three points at the top of the table.

As I pointed out in Monday's Sportsday, and sorry for the repetition if you're a subscriber (if not you can join us here ) City welcome Pepe Guardiola back to the Etihad tonight: "Although the six-time title winning manager will be there, solely he maintains, as a supporter and may well be seen shaking his inflatable banana, getting the badge in and even twisting his melon, man, he is also there as a support, steadfast in his belief in the club and their integrity. Watch him turn spectating into a symbolic act."

articles.title: Infantino faces showdown with internal critics as deadline for challengers nears
articles.summary: The FIFA president will have to answer for some of his most controversial decisions including the Trump Peace Prize and plan to sell World Cup shares.
articles.body:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino will face his strongest internal critics Thursday as he seeks to shore up support ahead of a Nov. 18 deadline for challengers to declare their intention to run against him.

The Zurich meeting will be Infantino's first in-person encounter with the full FIFA Council since Infantino's plan to create a commercial subsidiary of the organization with President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, as a key investor. The proposal, called FIFA Forward Enterprise, was mothballed in the face of insurmountable backlash. "He's got to come out of this calming the waters — he's not gonna calm everybody, but he absolutely has to settle some of his bigger critics right now," said a person involved in global soccer at the highest levels, granted anonymity to speak candidly about internal matters. "Because if he falls or trips, I think it'll really be a setback for him."

The agenda for the meeting opens with remarks by Infantino and routine business, including a review of the 2026 World Cup, before turning to areas that could find FIFA's president at odds with the 37 members of the organization's main decision-making body. That includes the FIFA Peace Prize awarded to Trump last December, the failed FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal and the organization's disciplinary procedures, which could raise questions about Infantino's dealings with the White House around a red card issued to an American player during the World Cup.

"All the meaty stuff is at the very end," the person said. "He'll get through, but his wings will be clipped."

Among the critics Infantino must face are UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin, Concacaf President Victor Montagliani and Asian Football Confederation President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa. All three lead confederations that have called on Infantino to resign while demanding an independent review of FIFA's governance.

Infantino has spent the nearly three months since the FIFA Forward proposal imploded working to steady his position. He has nodded to the need for an external review and continued a campaign of personal diplomacy, including trips to Colombia for the inauguration of President Abelardo de la Espriella and to the Caribbean Football Union's Under-14 Challenge Series in the Dominican Republic in August, which made for an awkward encounter with Montagliani , who urged him to stay away, according to media reports.

UEFA had threatened a boycott over the FIFA Forward proposal, but ultimately backed away from the threat. And Infantino is finding other ways to shore up support, particularly among developing countries where he's already built strong coalitions.

For instance, FIFA, this week, is proposing a $3.4 billion increase in development funding for member associations.

Infantino has also managed to keep much of his inner circle intact, including FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström, who remains in his post despite expressing concerns about Infantino's close association with Trump.

The governance fight is unfolding alongside a push by European Football Clubs, formerly the European Club Association, to expand its influence beyond 920 clubs across 55 countries and territories. At its general assembly in Copenhagen on Sept. 29, Chair Nasser Al-Khelaïfi announced a study of the feasibility of creating a global organization for clubs, provisionally called World Football Clubs. Such a group, whose members would control the players necessary to stage international tournaments, could serve as a powerful counterweight to FIFA.

Al-Khelaïfi has been seen as a promising candidate for FIFA's presidency, but he has said he is not interested. So far, retired Swiss defender Ramon Vega has emerged as the only challenger to Infantino in his bid for a fourth full term, which will be decided in an election of FIFA's 211 member nations next March.

articles.title: Maresca felt Man City deserved something from PSG defeat
articles.summary: Enzo Maresca believes Manchester City deserved to get something out of a wild 4-2 Champions League loss to Paris St Germain after fighting back from 3-0 down...
articles.body:
Enzo Maresca believes Manchester City deserved to get something out of a wild 4-2 Champions League loss to Paris St Germain after fighting back from 3-0 down in a chaotic second half.

In their first home game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules, and with former manager Pep Guardiola watching on, City lost for the first time since the Community Shield defeat to Arsenal in August, a run of eight games.

PSG ripped them apart in the first half, storming ahead through quickfire goals from Desire Doue and Ousmane Dembele, then all but killing it when Vitinha made it 3-0 with 32 minutes gone.

A triple change at the break helped rouse City as Erling Haaland scored twice, becoming City's record goalscorer in the Champions League in the process as he moved to 38 goals from 41 appearances, while also hitting the crossbar and seeing Enzo Fernandez denied by the post.

But in between Haaland's strikes, Maghnes Akliouche scored PSG's fourth, the ball squeezing past a despairing Gianluigi Donnarumma, and a comeback proved beyond Maresca's men even if former City man Ferran Torres missed a late penalty for the visitors.

"(It) has been a bit of a strange game, especially because we concede two goals in two minutes that create some problems for us," Maresca said. "Before the first goal we didn't concede nothing, we had some good moments then after two minutes, we concede the second one so it becomes more difficult.

"Then I think in the second half we did enough to deserve something more.

"The reason for me we struggle in first half is we concede two goals and when you are inside the pitch you know it's already difficult against them and you think 'Oh my God'.

"But second half I think we create enough chances to deserve something more. Luis (Enrique) also told me at the end they have been quite lucky in the 90 minutes, but again we lost, we can learn from that and we move on."

Maresca admitted the speed at which PSG hit his side, with only 99 seconds separating Doue's long-range strike and Dembele's header, rocked his team.

"At half-time the message was that the reason we lost the balance of the first half was because we conceded two goals," he said.

"And then the message was exactly the same message as before the game - these types of teams, if you don't go toe to toe you struggle. You have to be brave, you have to go."

City had won their first match after being hit with the guilty verdict by going to Anfield and taking apart a Liverpool side reduced to 10 men as they won 3-0, but there was a very different feeling at the Etihad when they players went in at half-time trailing by the same scoreline.

Maresca, who said he had not spoken to Guardiola before the match, denied this was a case of events catching up with his players.

articles.title: Guardiola's return, Man City's defiance - and a game of glorious chaos
articles.summary: On their return to Etihad Stadium Manchester City put on a show of defiance - even in the face of a PSG masterclass, writes Phil McNulty.
articles.body:
Manchester City returned to the welcoming surroundings of home for the first time since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations awash with defiance and presenting an 'us against the world' united front.

Pep Guardiola was back at the place he decorated with success for a decade in a public show of support to embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and chief executive Ferran Soriano, the Catalan a low-key presence clad in a flat cap sitting a row behind the pair.

If his appearance was relatively under the radar, the fact that he chose a game certain to attract a global audience to make his return was heavy with significance.

Guardiola is ignoring the outside noise to back his former bosses to clear their name on appeal after the guilty verdict passed down by an independent commission.

The stand bearing his name was emblazoned with a 'CTID' - City 'Til I Die - mosaic, while the build-up to kick-off saw a display of fireworks and pyrotechnics worthy of several rock concerts.

The strategy to show an unabashed City ready to face down any enemy was going well, until the game kicked off and Champions League holders Paris St-Germain produced a ruthless first-half reality check cloaked within the brutal beauty of their football.

With City providing a dramatic backdrop off the pitch, the game more than matched the setting. A second-half revival ensured embarrassment was avoided - and instead gave us a classic.

City's first step back into the limelight on the hostile territory of Anfield on Sunday ended with a 3-0 win at Liverpool and wild celebrations.

Here, with Guardiola watching on from the directors' box with an agonised expression mirroring that of successor Enzo Maresca in his technical area, City ran headlong into a whirlwind of magnificent football from Luis Enrique's PSG, the half-time scoreline of 3-0 actually doing them a kindness.

To City's great credit, and also Maresca's after he made three half-time changes, they responded superbly after the break, creating a host of chances before eventually losing 4-2.

It did not retrieve what was lost in the first half, but it did at least allow City's fans to ramp up a frenzied atmosphere and give their team a rousing send-off at the final whistle.

In these surroundings, there was no question of any backlash against City's Abu Dhabi-based owners, despite the fact they were found guilty of such serious financial charges to leave the club in crisis and attracting pariah status.

The damage was done in PSG's staggering opening 45 minutes, with Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha the scorers as City were ripped apart.

A game that began in a wall of sound, with Guardiola's name resounding around the stadium at kick-off, was reduced to stunned silence in the first 15 minutes.

City, so composed and ordered amid the toxicity of Anfield on Sunday, were shell-shocked on home territory as even born streetfighters such as Enzo Fernandez were reduced to chasing shadows.

The players who rose in the face of the storm raging around Manchester City at Liverpool suddenly looked like they were carrying the weight of the world on their shoulders, which made their outstanding display after the break even more praiseworthy.

Guardiola looked just as engaged as when he was manager

Erling Haaland gave City hope, which looked to be snuffed out when goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, who had a very poor night against his former club, saved from Maghnes Akliouche, only to see the ball drop behind him into the net.

Guardiola sometimes looked just as engaged as he did when he prowled the touchline here at Etihad Stadium, collecting the trophies now being called into question.

When Josko Gvardiol had a header cleared off the line Guardiola clutched his face in anguish. When Haaland scored a goal that threatened to offer City an unlikely lifeline, he remained seated but pumped his fists into the air.

If the Catalan was a neutral observer, he would have relished a game of glorious chaos, the first half embellished by PSG before City mounted superb momentum after the break.

As a lover of pure football with the emphasis placed firmly on attack, he may have enjoyed it anyway. The post-match discussion with Maresca would certainly have had a busy agenda.

Maresca felt he saw enough to give City hope should they meet PSG again later in the Champions League, despite the manner in which they were dismantled in the first half.

"I really like playing against PSG because they are brave," said Maresca. "We know the way they want to press. They go man-to-man and they are very dynamic on the ball. They are the best team in Europe. They play fantastic football.

"But I think we are there. The reason why we struggled was because we conceded two early goals so quickly. When you are on the pitch you might think this is difficult, but in the second half we created enough to maybe deserve something.

"We feel sorry for the first half but I think we're quite happy now."

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha, watching for Match of the Day, described it as "great entertainment", but "not a normal game of football".

"I don't feel like both teams were going at it at the same time," he said. "In the first half, PSG were excellent and City looked really off the pace. As a consequence they were heavily punished and the game basically left them.

"But then in the second half they have made some changes, they have rallied, knowing they are playing in front of their own crowd and their performance had to be better. So, it was more aggressive and more on the front foot, and that's why we saw those crazy scenes where it was shot after shot by City.

"If these two teams had played this game in matchweek six or seven, it would not have looked like this. There would have been more defensive solidity from both sides and they would probably have approached the game in a different manner.

"But at this stage, as we have kind of seen with some of the other games tonight, it is just goals, goals and more goals."

Either way, the superb Enrique remains the scourge of the Premier League, adding another win against City to a Champions League victims list that includes Liverpool, Aston Villa, Tottenham Hotspur and Arsenal, in a semi-final then last season's final.

Enrique is currently master of all he surveys in Europe as leader of this wonderful PSG team.

For Maresca and City, it is back to domestic business at home to Ipswich Town on Saturday – and all the uncertainty that brings with the Premier League in a state of limbo as they await sanctions and the result of their appeal.
authors: Phil McNulty - Chief football writer at Etihad Stadium

articles.title: Martinez outburst came out of 'anger and frustration'
articles.summary: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez says he "spoke out of anger and frustration" when launching a scathing attack on the club's hierarchy.
articles.body:
Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez says he "spoke out of anger and frustration" when launching a scathing attack on the club's hierarchy.

The Argentina international criticised United for not strengthening the squad in the summer following qualification for the Champions League in comments made after the 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid in the Champions League group phase on Tuesday.

Martinez said he expected more investment in the United squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]".

However, while he stopped short of an apology, he said he has "belief in my team-mates, our manager [Michael Carrick] and everyone working to help this club move forward".

"After the match, I spoke out of anger and frustration at not getting the result we all wanted," he wrote in a social media post.

"Those who know me know how I live football, with passion, commitment and a huge desire to win. And when things don't go our way, it hurts, especially when representing a club with the history and stature of Manchester United.

"My words reflect how I feel and how much I want to see this club competing for the biggest honours.

"Those high standards are part of how I see football and the responsibility that comes with wearing this shirt.

"When I talk about wanting more, I'm talking about the ambition we must all have as part of this club.

"To keep growing, to become stronger and to have everything we need to compete at the highest level.

"These are standards we must all hold ourselves to, starting with me."

Manchester United have not won in five games since beating Sabah in the Champions League on 10 September.

They have won just two of their nine games this season and are 13th in the Premier League with six points from as many games.

Martinez's contract expires at the end of the season and United have the option to extend it by another year.

He added: "I know that, first and foremost, it's us, the players, who have to deliver, and I put myself at the front of that responsibility.

"We need to demand even more of ourselves and work together to take Manchester United back to the top.

"I believe in my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward.

"I'm convinced that the way forward is to keep working together, with ambition and commitment.

"My goal has been the same since day one, to win, compete at the highest level and to give everything I have for this badge."

Manchester United's next game will be at Leeds United in the Premier League on Sunday, 18 October.
